newsitem.title: UGANDA: Hillary promotes women's rights in Africa.
newsitem.headline: Hillary promotes women's rights in Africa.

text.p: Heading into the final stretch of her two-week Africa tour, U.S. first lady Hillary Rodham Clinton says she hopes she has helped promote a "growing awareness" among African governments of women's rights.

President Clinton's wife will have another opportunity to talk about the need to provide women and children with better health care and education opportunities on Friday when she delivers a speech to members of the Ugandan parliament, women, students and faculty from the Makerere University.

She will have some reason to celebrate. U.S. officials credit Uganda with the having one of the most progressive political programmes for women in Africa. A new constitution in 1995 required that at least 14 percent of parliamentary seats and one-third of elected local government offices be filled by women.

But plenty of obstacles from the U.S. standpoint remain. U.S. officials say the typical Ugandan woman bears 6.9 children in her lifetime and has limited access to pre-natal care, leading to high maternal mortality. And the rate of AIDS infection is higher in women than men.
Mrs. Clinton, speaking to reporters on Thursday in northern Tanzania, said she has raised women's issues with leaders of governments in Africa during her visit and has not met a negative response.

She said during her visit to the Tanzanian capital, Dar es Salaam, earlier this week, she talked to Tanzanian President Benjamin Mkapa about proposed legislation there concerning extension of property rights and inheritance rights to women.
She said change is difficult -- in America as well as in Africa.

But she said based on the discussions she has had with prominent women in each country, "I think there is now a growing awareness and a movement to match that awareness...that is really going to put women's issues on the agenda here in Africa."

During her day on Friday, Mrs. Clinton planned a visit to the Seguku Primary School to underscore the need to educate children. She also planned a visit to an AIDS information centre. It is estimated that more than 1.5 million Ugandans are infected with the deadly virus.
She also planned to visit Bwaise Village to promote a U.S. government programme that promotes lending small amounts of money to women entrepreneurs.
To call attention to the plight of women afflicted by the genocide in Rwanda, she was to participate in a discussion with women from Rwanda.
Mrs. Clinton, accompanied by her 17-year-old daughter Chelsea, was welcomed on her arrival from Tanzania on Thursday with large crowds lining her motorcade route.

Uganda was the fifth of six countries she will visit on her goodwill mission, with Eritrea remaining as the last. She goes there on Saturday for a brief visit and gets back to Washington early Sunday.
Besides Tanzania, she has also visited Senegal, South Africa and Zimbabwe.
